title: A boulder plummets and grit drifts — they used to do neither
question: Does the descent read at the right pace now? And is 'big pieces lead, grit trails' better or worse than everything arriving together?
context_md:
*"Still reads as too fast."* — and you asked what is realistic. Here is what physics says, and it turned out to name a specific missing thing rather than a number to lower.

**Nothing in the model knew how big a piece was.** The speed limit I added scaled with density only, so a boulder and a grain of grit sank at exactly the same speed. The readout that says so is new, and it is blunt: on the same drop, *"smallest piece 4 cells across at 1.76, largest 17 across at 1.75"*.

Real terminal velocity balances weight-minus-buoyancy against drag, and works out to **the square root of the body's size**. Measured in a deep tank:

| body, cells across | 3 | 8 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 1.75 | 1.75 | 1.75 |
| **now** | **0.82** | **1.34** | **1.90** |

Those three numbers are the closed-form answer to two decimal places — nothing fitted. A typical piece in this drop is 4 to 8 cells across, so the pieces that dominate what you see slow by **30 to 45%**.

**This deliberately un-does part of what you asked for last time**, and I want to be straight about it. You said pieces arrived at different times; I made them all arrive together. That was over-correcting. What was actually wrong then was a **43x** spread caused by nothing braking a body at all — pieces ordered by how long they had been falling, which means nothing. This is a **2.6x** spread ordered by *size*: the slab leads, the grit trails. If it now reads as strung out again rather than as heavy-things-first, say so and I will pull the coefficient.

**What it costs.** Paired across four drop heights, stone converted to rubble: three of four unchanged or better, one clearly worse (-286 against -172). Total material lost from the world is lower at all four. Reported as measured rather than averaged into something flattering.

Two measurement traps on the way, both of which made a working fix look broken: peak speed over a body's whole life is its *entry* speed, not its sink speed — and filtering on "is it under water" is not enough either, because the harness looks after the body has moved, so a piece that entered this frame was in mid-air when the brake ran.

Both clips are the same drop at true speed.

items.label: before
items.caption: Every piece at 1.75 cells a frame, whatever its size.

items.label: now
items.caption: 0.82 for a 3-across fragment, 1.90 for a 16-across block.
